words: ما علمت لكم من إله غيري
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh habitually met Moses' proofs with a sophism meant to persuade the ignorant; here he advances two sophisms.
rows.anchor: كانت عادته متى ظهرت حجة موسى أن يتعلق في دفع تلك الحجة بشبهة يروجها على أغمار قومه

words: ما علمت لكم من إله غيري
rows.speaker: فرعون
rows.claim: Pharaoh's first sophism denies any other god because he claims there is no evidence; he says celestial bodies suffice to explain changes in the lower world, so no maker is needed.
rows.anchor: أما الأول فقد كان اعتماده على أن ما لا دليل عليه لم يجز إثباته

words: ما علمت لكم من إله غيري
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The premise that no proof exists is false: proof that bodies originated establishes that the heavens and stars originated, and every originated thing must have an originator, so the world has a maker.
rows.anchor: لأنا إذا عرفنا بالدليل حدوث الأجسام عرفنا حدوث الأفلاك والكواكب

words: ما علمت لكم من إله غيري
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some deniers turn failure to find evidence after searching into proof of nonexistence; Pharaoh was less extreme because he only withheld affirmation for lack of proof and suspected Moses was lying.
rows.anchor: فرجع حاصل كلامهم بعد التحقيق إلى أن كل ما لا يعرف عليه دليل وجب نفيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh's claim to be a deity did not mean he claimed to create the heavens, earth, seas, mountains, people, or their attributes; deity here means the one worshipped, and he claimed people owed obedience only to their king.
rows.anchor: بل الإله هو المعبود فالرجل كان ينفي الصانع ويقول لا تكليف على الناس إلا أن يطيعوا ملكهم وينقادوا لأمره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Against the common reading that Pharaoh claimed to create heaven and earth, al-Razi says Pharaoh knew God and made the claim to mislead the gullible, as he argued in his commentary on 20:49.
rows.anchor: على أنه كان عارفا بالله تعالى وأنه كان يقول ذلك ترويجا على الأغمار

rows.speaker: المشبهة
rows.claim: The anthropomorphists cite this verse to argue that God is in heaven; al-Razi replies that Moses called God Lord of heaven and earth without restricting Him to heaven, and Pharaoh maliciously distorted this.
rows.anchor: تعلقت المشبهة بهذه الآية في أن الله تعالى في السماء قالوا لولا أن موسى عليه السلام دعاه إلى ذلك

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: One account says Pharaoh built the tower: Haman assembled fifty thousand builders, besides laborers and attendants, to make bricks, plaster, timber, and nails, raising a structure higher than any before it.
rows.anchor: فال قوم إنه بناه قالوا إنه لما أمر ببناء الصرح جمع هامان العمال حتى اجتمع خمسون ألف بناء سوى الأتباع والأجراء

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: In that account Gabriel struck the tower at sunset and broke it into three pieces; one fell on Pharaoh's army and killed a million men, another into the sea, and another in the west, killing all the workers.
rows.anchor: فبعث الله تعالى جبريل عليه السلام عند غروب الشمس فضربه بجناحه فقطعه ثلاث قطع قطعة وقعت على عسكر فرعون فقتلت ألف ألف رجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further story says Pharaoh climbed the tower and shot an arrow toward heaven; it returned stained with blood, so he claimed to have killed Moses' God, after which Gabriel was sent to destroy the tower.
rows.anchor: ويروى في هذه القصة أن فرعون ارتقى فوقه ورمى بنشابة نحو السماء فأراد الله أن يفتنهم فردت إليهم وهي ملطوخة بالدم

rows.speaker: ومن الناس
rows.claim: Others say the tower was never built: rational people know climbing a tower cannot bring them nearer to heaven, since a person on a high mountain sees the sky as from the ground; an arrow cannot reach it either.
rows.anchor: ومن الناس من قال إنه لم يبن ذلك الصرح لأنه يبعد من العقلاء أن يظنوا أنهم بصعود الصرح يقربون من السماء مع علمهم بأن من على أعلى الجبال الشاهقة يرى السماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi rejects a literal account that violates necessary reason, since it would give attackers a strong pretext to disparage the Quran.
rows.anchor: يعرف فساده بضرورة العقل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi prefers that Pharaoh only pretended to build the tower, or that the order continued his claim that no proof of a maker exists: reason cannot prove it, nor can the senses without ascending heaven.
rows.anchor: فالأقرب أنه كان أوهم البناء ولم يبن أو كان هذا من تتمة قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On al-Razi's preferred reading, Pharaoh's tower order was mockery: after declaring that neither reason nor sensation could establish a creator, he concludes that Moses is a liar.
rows.anchor: وإنما قال ذلك على سبيل التهكم فبمجموع هذه الأشياء قرر أنه لا دليل على الصانع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh says to fire clay rather than simply to make bricks because he was the first brickmaker and knew the craft; the phrasing also suits Quranic eloquence and the speech of tyrants.
rows.anchor: ولم يقل اطبخ لي الآجر واتخذه لأنه أول من عمل الآجر فهو يعلمه الصنعة ولأن هذه العبارة أليق بفصاحة القرآن وأشبه بكلام الجبابرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling his minister Haman by name in the middle of the speech displays Pharaoh's self-exaltation and tyranny.
rows.anchor: بالإيقاد على الطين فنادى باسمه بيافي وسط الكلام دليل على التعظم والتجبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verbs ṭalaʿa and iṭṭalaʿ can both mean to ascend; one says either of ascending a mountain.
rows.anchor: والطلوع والاطلاع الصعود يقال طلع الجبل واطلع بمعنى واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only God may rightly be called al-Mutakabbir, the one possessing immense grandeur; every other being's self-exaltation is unjustified.
rows.anchor: الاستكبار بالحق إنما هو لله تعالى وهو المتكبر في الحقيقة أي المبالغ في كبرياء الشأن

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet quotes God as saying that pride is His cloak and greatness His garment, and that He casts into the Fire whoever contests either; al-Razi gives no grading.
rows.anchor: الكبرياء ردائي والعظمة إزاري ، فمن نازعني واحدا منهما ألقيته في النار

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubba'i argues that God did not grant Pharaoh kingship, since then it would be rightful; he applies this to usurpers and rejects the Umayyad rulers' claim that their rule came from God.
rows.anchor: قال الجبائي الآية تدل على أنه تعالى ما أعطاه الملك وإلا لكان ذلك بحق وهكذا كل متغلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi rejects al-Jubba'i's argument: if the ruler acquired power by himself, why could a weaker or less intelligent rival not do so; if God gave it, al-Jubba'i's conclusion follows; if people gave it, why did they unite behind one claimant and abandon the other?
rows.anchor: واعلم أن هذا ضعيف لأن وصول ذلك الملك إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh and his troops knew God but denied the resurrection; this is why they rebelled and transgressed.
rows.anchor: فهذا يدل على أنهم كانوا عارفين بالله تعالى إلا أنهم كانوا ينكرون البعث فلأجل ذلك تمردوا وطغوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Casting Pharaoh and his numerous troops into the sea pictures them as mere pebbles tossed from a handful, stressing how insignificant even a vast creation is beside God's power.
rows.anchor: شبههم استحقارا لهم واستقلالا لعددهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi frames the passage as God questioning the unbelievers about three matters on Resurrection Day; first He asks where their alleged partners are.
rows.anchor: اعلم أنه سبحانه وتعالى ذكر في هذه الآية أنه يسأل الكفار يوم القيامة عن ثلاثة أشياء أحدها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: By then the unbelievers know by necessity that their former practice was false and that monotheism and prophethood are true; God asks where the objects they worshipped and claimed would intercede are, and who will now rescue them.
rows.anchor: لما ثبت أن الكفار يوم القيامة قد عرفوا بطلان ما كانوا عليه وعرفوا صحة التوحيد والنبوة بالضرورة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The “word” whose implication has become binding is God's promise to fill Hell with jinn and humans.
rows.anchor: معنى حق عليه القول أي حق عليه مقتضاه

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One reported identification of those on whom the punishment-word is binding is the leaders who summoned people to misguidance.
rows.anchor: فقال بعضهم الرؤساء الدعاة إلى الضلال

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another reported identification of those on whom the punishment-word is binding is the devils.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم الشياطين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In “these whom we misled,” “these” is the subject, “whom we misled” its adjective, the relative's pronoun is omitted, and “we misled them” is the predicate; the comparison modifies an omitted verbal noun.
rows.anchor: هؤلاء مبتدأ والذين أغوينا صفته والراجع إلى الموصوف محذوف وأغويناهم الخبر والكاف صفة مصدر محذوف تقديره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The misleaders mean that their influence did not compel anyone: their followers chose their own beliefs and actions, just as the misleaders chose their own error.
rows.anchor: والمراد كما أن غينا باختيارنا فكذا غيهم باختيارهم يعني أن أغواءنا لهم ما ألجأهم إلى الغواية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi links this denial of coercion to Satan's statement that he only invited people and they answered, and to God's statement that Satan has no authority over servants except those who follow him.
rows.anchor: هذا معنى ما حكاه الله عن الشيطان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The misleaders disavow their followers' beliefs and deeds, saying they worshipped their own desires, as followers later disavow those they followed.
rows.anchor: تبرأنا إليك منهم ومن عقائدهم وأعمالهم ما كانوا إيانا يعبدون إنما كانوا يعبدون أهواءهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alleged partners may be the human leaders or devils: by obeying them, people effectively made them partners; those leaders can answer that people followed corrupt desires rather than worshipping them.
rows.anchor: أن يريد به هؤلاء الرؤساء والشياطين فإنهم لما أطاعوهم

words: وقيل ادعوا شركاءكم فدعوهم فلم يستجيبوا لهم
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to call the partners is chiefly a reproach, since the unbelievers know the partners cannot help; their failure to answer leaves punishment certain and warns people in this life.
rows.anchor: لأنهم يعلمون أنه لا فائدة في دعائهم لهم

rows.speaker: الضحاك ومقاتل
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak and Muqatil take the omitted consequence to mean that the followers and followed see the punishment; had they been guided in worldly life, they would not see it in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: قال الضحاك ومقاتل يعني المتبوع والتابع يرون العذاب ولو أنهم كانوا يهتدون في الدنيا ما أبصروه في الآخرة

rows.speaker: كثير من المفسرين
rows.claim: A second proposed completion is that, had they been guided in worldly life, they would have known the punishment was true.
rows.anchor: لو أنهم كانوا مهتدين في الدنيا لعلموا أن العذاب حق

rows.speaker: كثير من المفسرين
rows.claim: A third proposed completion is that when they see the punishment they will wish they had been guided in worldly life.
rows.anchor: ودوا حين رأوا العذاب لو كانوا في الدنيا يهتدون

rows.speaker: كثير من المفسرين
rows.claim: A fourth proposed completion is that they would have warded off the punishment if they had known any stratagem for doing so.
rows.anchor: لو كانوا يهتدون لوجه من وجوه الحيل لدفعوا به العذاب

rows.speaker: كثير من المفسرين
rows.claim: A fifth completion says it is now time for them to be guided when they see the punishment, supported by the verse that they will not believe until they see painful punishment.
rows.anchor: قد آن لهم أن يهتدوا لو أنهم كانوا يهتدون إذا رأوا العذاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi argues that the consequence of “if only they were guided” is not omitted; one reading is that the command to call their partners fills them with terror and dizziness, blinding them so they cannot see the punishment.
rows.anchor: فههنا يشتد الخوف عليهم ويلحقهم شيء كالسدر والدوار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second reading takes the pronoun in “they saw” to refer to the idols: they would see the punishment if they were living and guided, but are not; the pronoun is acceptable because the preceding wording reflects the unbelievers' belief.
rows.anchor: أي هذه الأصنام كانوا يشاهدون العذاب لو كانوا من الأحياء المهتدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third reading makes “seeing” inward: the unbelievers knew in worldly life that the punishment was true, had they been guided.
rows.anchor: أن يكون المراد من الرؤية رؤية القلب أي والكفار علموا حقية هذا العذاب في الدنيا لو كانوا يهتدون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi considers these direct readings better than supplying an omitted consequence, which would break the verse's arrangement.
rows.anchor: وهذه الوجوه عندي خير من الوجوه المبنية على أن جواب لو محذوف فإن ذلك يقتضي تفكيك النظم من الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When asked what they answered the messengers, all the reports become inaccessible to them, like something blind; they cannot find an answer or ask one another because all are equally confused and helpless.
rows.anchor: أي فصارت الأنباء كالعمى عليهم جميعا لا تهتدي إليهم فهم لا يتساءلون لا يسأل بعضهم بعضا كما يتساءل الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi notes an alternative reading of “the reports became confused/blind upon them,” without naming its reciter.
rows.anchor: وقرىء فعميت وإذا كانت الأنبياء لهول ذلك يتعتعون في الجواب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even prophets will stammer from awe when asked this question and defer to God's knowledge, as in the gathering when God asks the messengers what response they received.
rows.anchor: يتعتعون في الجواب عن مثل هذا السؤال ، ويفوضون الأمر إلى علم الله

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: The Qadi argues this verse disproves determinism: if God created unbelief irresistibly, the unbelievers could blame Him for creating their denial and would have a compelling defense, as could Satan.
rows.anchor: قال القاضي هذه الآية تدل على بطلان القول بالجبر لأن فعلهم لو كان خلقا من الله تعالى ويجب وقوعه بالقدرة والإرادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi says the Qadi repeats the same argument from verses of praise, blame, reward, and punishment; his own reply is that God's knowing they will not believe and their believing are mutually impossible, so commanding belief would command opposites.
rows.anchor: وكما أن وجه استدلاله في الكل هذا الحرف فكذا وجه جوابنا حرف واحد وهو أن علم الله تعالى بعدم الإيمان مع وقوع الإيمان متنافيان لذاتيهما

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: In his theological books the Qadi says one should neither call the demanded act possible nor impossible, but remain silent; if an unbeliever raised the objection to God, God could only be silent, leaving the unbeliever's excuse strong.
rows.anchor: والذي اعتمد القاضي عليه في دفع هذا الحرف في كتبه الكلامية قوله خطأ قول من يقول إنه يمكن وخطأ قول من يقول إنه لا يمكن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi concludes that the determinist and anti-determinist positions face the same difficulty, so the objection and excuse remain strong whichever side is taken.
rows.anchor: فتكون حجة الكافر قوية وعذره ظاهرا فثبت أن الإشكال مشترك والله أعلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After first condemning the polytheists and then presenting monotheism and its proofs, God returns to condemning their way and describes their state in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: عاد إلى تهجين طريقتهم مرة أخرى وشرح حالهم في الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On Resurrection Day God asks where the beings whose divinity they claimed are, or where their claim that they sought nearness to God is; they know only God is divine, so the question deepens their grief.
rows.anchor: وقد علموا أن لا إله إلا الله فيكون ذلك زائدا في غمهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God selects one witness from every community to testify against it.
rows.anchor: فالمراد ميزنا واحدا ليشهد عليهم

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One view identifies the witnesses as prophets, who testify that they delivered the proofs and clarified them fully, showing that the people's failure was their own and increasing their grief.
rows.anchor: ثم قال بعضهم هم الأنبياء يشهدون بأنهم بلغوا القوم الدلائل وبلغوا في إيضاحها كل غاية

rows.speaker: آخرون
rows.claim: Others identify them as witnesses who testify about people in every era, including prophets; al-Razi prefers this broader view because it includes periods without a prophet and periods after Muhammad, when people will know the truth belongs to God and His messengers.
rows.anchor: وقال آخرون بل هم الشهداء الذين يشهدون على الناس في كل زمان ويدخل في جملتهم الأنبياء وهذا أقرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What they used to fabricate and lie about disappears from them as a lost thing.
rows.anchor: غاب عنهم غيبة الشيء الضائع

words: إن قارون كان من قوم موسى
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse says Qarun belonged to Moses' people, which may imply that he believed in Moses; it may instead indicate kinship.
rows.anchor: ظاهر ذلك يدل على أنه كان ممن قد أمن به

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says Qarun was Moses' cousin, giving their shared ancestry through Yishar, Qohath, and Levi.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي : إنه كان ابن عم موسى عليه السلام

rows.speaker: محمد بن إسحاق
rows.claim: Muhammad ibn Ishaq says Qarun was Moses' paternal uncle, based on their shared ancestry through Yishar and Qohath.
rows.anchor: وقال محمد بن إسحاق إنه كان عم موسى عليه السلام

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says Qarun was Moses' maternal cousin.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس أنه كان ابن خالته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qarun was called al-Munawwar for his handsome appearance and was Israel's foremost reciter of the Torah, but he became a hypocrite like al-Samiri.
rows.anchor: ثم قيل إنه كان يسمى المنور لحسن صورته وكان أقرأ بني إسرائيل للتوراة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation is that Qarun's wealth made him despise the poor, disregard their right as fellow believers, and fail to honor them.
rows.anchor: أنه استخف بالفقراء ولم يرع لهم حق الإيمان ولا عظمهم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation is that Qarun acted unjustly; Pharaoh had appointed him over the Israelites, whom he then oppressed.
rows.anchor: أنه من الظلم ، قيل ملكه فرعون على

rows.speaker: القفال
rows.claim: Al-Qaffal explains that Qarun sought superiority over his people and wanted them subjected to him.
rows.anchor: قال القفال : بغى عليهم

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak says Qarun transgressed, overpowered his people, and did not deal fairly with them.
rows.anchor: قال الضحاك : طغى عليهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains that Qarun acted tyrannically and arrogantly toward his people and angered them.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس : تجبر وتكبر عليهم

rows.speaker: شهر بن حوشب
rows.claim: Shahr ibn Hawshab says Qarun's transgression was to wear clothes a span longer than his people's, an act of arrogance.
rows.anchor: قال شهر بن حوشب : بغيه عليهم أنه زاد عليهم في الثياب شبرا

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says Qarun envied Aaron's high-priestly office: Moses had prophecy and Aaron the priesthood, altar, and offerings, while Qarun felt he had no position.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي : بغيه عليهم أنه حسد هرون على الحبورة

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: In al-Kalbi's account, Moses tested the leaders' rods by God's command; Aaron's almond-wood rod sprouted green leaves overnight, but Qarun called the sign magic and withdrew with many followers.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي : بغيه عليهم أنه حسد هرون على الحبورة

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi's story continues that Aaron received the priesthood, altar, and offerings; Israelites brought him gifts, which a heavenly fire consumed, while wealthy Qarun separated with many Israelite followers.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي : بغيه عليهم أنه حسد هرون على الحبورة

words: إن قارون كان من قوم موسى
rows.speaker: أبو أمامة الباهلي
rows.claim: Abu Umama al-Bahili reports that the Prophet said Qarun was among the seventy chosen ones who heard God's speech; al-Razi gives no grading.
rows.anchor: وروى أبو أمامة الباهلي عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: الكعبي
rows.claim: Al-Kaʿbi objects that if God does not give illicit wealth, the phrase “We gave him” conflicts with that principle; al-Razi replies that the text does not establish Qarun's wealth was illicit, and it could have come from previous kings' treasure, inheritance, or trade.
rows.anchor: قال الكعبي : ألستم تقولون إن الله لا يعطي الحرام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mafātih is the plural of maftaḥ, with a kasra on the mīm, meaning keys; it is also said to mean stores, whose singular would be maftaḥ with a fatḥa.
rows.anchor: المفاتح جمع مفتح بكسر الميم وهو ما يفتح به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The idiom nāʾa bihi al-ḥiml means that a load became so heavy it made its bearer lean.
rows.anchor: ويقال ناء به الحمل إذا أثقله حتى أماله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿUṣba means a large group and is synonymous with ʿiṣāba; the brothers of Joseph were ten, since Joseph and his brother were not with them.
rows.anchor: والعصبة الجماعة الكثيرة والعصابة مثلها

rows.speaker: قائلون
rows.claim: One interpretation takes the keys literally: each storehouse had a finger-sized key made of camel hide, and sixty camels carried the keys when Qarun rode.
rows.anchor: قالوا كانت مفاتيحه من جلود الإبل وكل مفتاح مثل إصبع

rows.speaker: بعض الناس
rows.claim: Critics of the literal-key view object that one person's wealth would not require so many keys, and that buried treasure would have no keys.
rows.anchor: ومن الناس من طعن في هذا القول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi answers that a great volume of goods rather than coin could require many keys; the report of sixty loads is not in the Quran and should not be accepted, while numerous distinct keys would be hard for a group to track.
rows.anchor: أن المال إذا كان من جنس العروض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although “treasures” conventionally means wealth stored underground, it can also denote collected wealth kept in places secured by locks.
rows.anchor: أن ظاهر الكنز وإن كان من جهة العرف ما قالوا فقد يقع على المال المجموع في المواضع التي عليها أغلاق

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan prefer taking the keys metaphorically as the wealth itself, which they consider clearer and farther from the objections; Ibn Abbas says forty strong men carried Qarun's treasuries, which numbered four hundred thousand, ten thousand per carrier.
rows.anchor: وهو اختيار ابن عباس والحسن أن تحمل المفاتح على نفس المال

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abu Muslim takes mafātih to mean knowledge and comprehensive access, as in “with Him are the keys of the unseen”; Qarun's varied, abundant treasures burdened their keepers' ability to preserve and oversee them.
rows.anchor: اختيار أبي مسلم : أن المراد من المفاتح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qarun's people tell him not to rejoice with such vanity and worldly attachment that it distracts him altogether from the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: والمراد لا يلحقه من البطر والتمسك بالدنيا ما يلهيه عن أمر الآخرة أصلا

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some say only someone content with and settled in worldly life rejoices in it; one who knows he will soon leave does not, as al-Mutanabbi aptly observed.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم : إنه لا يفرح بالدنيا إلا من رضي بها
